subtype: College sleep debt and mood swings [Actor]
passage: At the agricultural college hostel outside Dharwad, Parul's nights ran on chai from the gate stall and chats until three. She slept through the eight o'clock lecture twice a week and felt flat all afternoon. On Thursday she cried because a senior didn't reply to her message, and on Friday she shouted at Bhupen for borrowing her notes. 'What's wrong with me? Maybe I need a new timetable app,' she groaned. Bhupen, from the next village, grinned. 'Maybe you need sleep. Try lights off by midnight for one week. No chai after dinner.' Grumbling, she tried it. By the next Thursday she made the eight o'clock lecture and laughed at Bhupen's jokes again.

qa.q: What did Bhupen suggest?
qa.a: Lights off by midnight for one week, and no chai after dinner.

qa.q: How was Parul feeling during the late-night weeks?
qa.a: She felt flat and anxious, crying over an unanswered message and snapping at Bhupen without linking it to sleep.

qa.q: What small change lifted Parul's mood?
qa.a: Lights off by midnight and no chai after dinner, so her sleep became more regular.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when Parul shouted about the notes?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt stung for a moment, but stayed kind and saw the tiredness behind it.

grounding: A hostel student running on late nights and chai feels flat and snappy, and small regular sleep changes lift her mood.

subtype: Roommate living with a night owl [Receiver]
passage: Arnab, you're complaining about your roommate's lamp at two in the morning? Let your Uday Mama tell you about Kallol. In our engineering hostel, Kallol studied at night with a radio, a table lamp and endless calls from the phone booth downstairs. I lay awake, fuming, and never said a word. I just slammed my cupboard in the mornings and left sarcastic notes about 'some people'. By the second term we weren't speaking, and I was doing badly in tests from lack of sleep. Then one night I finally said it plainly: 'Kallol, the lamp and the radio keep me awake. Can we find a way?' He was shocked; he'd had no idea. He bought a clip-on lamp and earphones, and I got an eye mask. We stayed friends for forty years.

qa.q: What did Kallol buy after the talk?
qa.a: A clip-on lamp and earphones.

qa.q: How did young Uday feel lying awake?
qa.a: He felt resentful and angry, fuming silently while Kallol's lamp and radio kept him up.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Uday's hostel story?
qa.a: The night he named the problem plainly and asked for a way, which led to a clip-on lamp, earphones and an eye mask.

qa.q: How did Kallol feel when Uday finally spoke up?
qa.a: Kallol was shocked, having had no idea the lamp and radio were a problem.

grounding: An uncle recalls how silent resentment towards a night-owl roommate grew until a specific request and compromise ended it.

passage: Gabriel, two years into a consulting job in Sao Paulo, liked boasting about how little he slept. He answered emails at one in the morning and was at his desk by seven, proud of it. By June his coffee count had doubled. In a client meeting he snapped at Wei, his teammate, over a small slide error, then made a bigger one himself: he quoted last year's figures. Afterwards Wei found him staring at the lift doors. 'You're working longer and getting worse,' Wei said quietly. 'That's not dedication, that's debt.' The words stung, but Gabriel checked his own error log. It was true. He began shutting his laptop at eleven.

qa.q: What mistake did Gabriel make in the client meeting?
qa.a: He quoted last year's figures.

qa.q: How did Gabriel feel when Wei called it debt?
qa.a: He felt stung, but when he checked his own error log he saw it was true.

qa.q: What did Gabriel change?
qa.a: He began shutting his laptop at eleven to protect his sleep.

qa.q: What is it like for Wei to be snapped at over a small slide error?
qa.a: Wei probably felt hurt and unfairly treated, yet chose to speak honestly and kindly afterwards.

grounding: A young professional treats short sleep as dedication until irritability and errors show it is lowering his performance.

passage:
Team lead's note to self, Wednesday
Disha is usually the sharpest person on our team and the one who makes everyone laugh at stand-up. For two weeks now: three small mistakes in the invoices, jokes gone flat, and today she snapped at Arvind for asking a simple question. Someone in the pantry called her 'moody lately'. I shut that down. At four I asked Disha for a quiet coffee, just the two of us, and asked how she was doing, not about the errors. She admitted she has been taking late-night calls with the overseas team and sleeping badly. We moved those calls to a colleague for a fortnight. I'll check in again on Friday.
Nikita

qa.q: What had Disha been doing that affected her sleep?
qa.a: Taking late-night calls with the overseas team.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when someone called Disha 'moody lately'?
qa.a: Nikita felt protective and uncomfortable with the gossip, and chose to shut it down.

qa.q: Why was a private coffee better than criticising the invoice mistakes?
qa.a: It let Disha explain the real cause, poor sleep from late calls, so a practical fix could be found.

qa.q: What might Disha have felt being asked how she was doing instead of about the errors?
qa.a: Disha likely felt relieved and respected, which made it easier to admit she was sleeping badly.

grounding: A team lead notices a sharp colleague's mistakes and flat humour and checks in privately about workload and rest.

subtype: Persistent insomnia and knowing when to seek help [Response]
passage: For five weeks Maria, the young English teacher at the school in Kumta, had lain awake till two. She had tried everything: warm milk, no phone after nine, the same wake time, a dark room with the fan on. Still she stared at the ceiling, and in the daytime a heavy worry sat on her chest. She didn't want to make a fuss. Her landlady, Ganga, found her crying over a stack of corrections. 'Enough, child. This is not something to push through alone.' The next morning Ganga went with her to the doctor at the taluk hospital. Maria kept her steady wake time and dark room, and began talking about the worry too.

qa.q: Where did Ganga go with Maria?
qa.a: To the doctor at the taluk hospital.

qa.q: Why hadn't Maria sought help sooner?
qa.a: She felt reluctant to make a fuss and kept trying to push through, even while worry sat heavy on her chest.

qa.q: Why was seeing a doctor the wise next step?
qa.a: Weeks of poor sleep with daytime worry had not eased with good habits, so a doctor could help alongside her routine.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt finding Maria crying?
qa.a: Ganga probably felt worried and protective, deciding Maria shouldn't face it alone.

grounding: A young teacher with weeks of poor sleep despite good habits stops pushing through and sees a doctor.

passage: The plumber came at noon, and lunch in the Chennai flat slid to half past one. Akash pushed away the banana Payal offered, then howled and threw his spoon. When she put rice on his tray, he swept it to the floor. 'Stop that!' she began, then looked at the clock. His lunch was over an hour late. She sat beside him, took a small spoonful of soft dal-rice and blew on it. Akash opened his mouth. Five spoons later he was smiling and banging the tray.

qa.q: What time did lunch slide to?
qa.a: Half past one.

qa.q: Why did Akash throw the spoon and sweep the rice away?
qa.a: He was hungry and miserable but couldn't say so, so his distress came out as crying and throwing.

qa.q: What worked better than 'Stop that!'?
qa.a: Payal noticed lunch was late and calmly fed him small spoonfuls, which ended the tantrum.

qa.q: What might Payal have felt when she looked at the clock?
qa.a: Payal likely felt a pang of guilt, realising Akash's meal was over an hour late.

grounding: A hungry toddler shows it by crying and throwing food, and feeding him ends the tantrum faster than discipline.

passage: At seven, dinner was still on the stove because Rashmi had come home late from work. Hemant, who had eaten nothing since his school tiffin, whined at every little thing. When his biscuit snapped in half, he burst into tears and hit his little sister's arm. 'Hemant! No hitting!' Rashmi said. He wailed louder. She took a breath, handed him a banana and sat him at the table. 'We'll talk after you eat.' Ten minutes later he patted his sister's arm, said sorry and asked to help lay the plates.

qa.q: What did Rashmi give Hemant?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: Why did Hemant burst into tears over a broken biscuit?
qa.a: He was very hungry, having eaten nothing since his school tiffin, so he felt cranky and small things upset him.

qa.q: Why did 'We'll talk after you eat' work?
qa.a: Food settled Hemant's body first, so he could then say sorry and help, which a lecture couldn't do.

qa.q: How might the little sister have felt when Hemant hit her?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and surprised, until he patted her arm and said sorry.

grounding: A young child whose dinner is late turns whiny and hits, and a small snack restores him better than a lecture.

passage:
Tuesday night
Strange afternoon. Alka, my quietest girl in Class 5, pushed Sameer off the bench after lunch and then argued with me about the maths homework, eyes flashing. I was about to send her to the corridor. Then I remembered her lunchbox at recess: two bites, then shut. When I asked, she muttered that she didn't like today's sabzi and wasn't hungry then. By three she clearly was. I gave her the spare biscuits from my drawer and a glass of water, and let her sit by the window. Twenty minutes later she apologised to Sameer on her own. Note to self: check lunchboxes, not just behaviour.
Pallavi

qa.q: What did Pallavi give Alka?
qa.a: The spare biscuits from the drawer and a glass of water.

qa.q: What was Pallavi about to do, and what made her pause?
qa.a: Pallavi felt irritated enough to send Alka to the corridor, then paused on remembering the lunchbox shut after two bites.

qa.q: What lesson did Pallavi take from the afternoon?
qa.a: To check lunchboxes, not just behaviour, since hunger can look like bad behaviour.

qa.q: How might Alka have been feeling by three o'clock?
qa.a: She was probably hungry and edgy, which made her quick to push and argue.

grounding: A teacher notices that a child who ate little at lunch is edgy and quarrelsome and treats the hunger instead of punishing.

subtype: Teen growth spurt appetite and grumpiness [Actor]
passage:
Farhan: why did u walk out of the group project call
Abhinav: sorry. I was being a jerk
Farhan: u called Mitali's idea dumb lol
Abhinav: I know. Hadn't eaten since lunch and practice went late. I was starving and everything felt annoying
Farhan: ur always hungry these days. U've grown so much since Diwali
Abhinav: Mom says it's a growth spurt thing. I get angry when I'm hungry now, it's weird
Farhan: so eat before calls?
Abhinav: yeah. Next time I'll just say 'give me 10 mins, food first, then we talk'
Abhinav: also messaging Mitali sorry now
Farhan: good 👍

qa.q: What will Abhinav say next time before a call?
qa.a: 'Give me 10 mins, food first, then we talk.'

qa.q: How was Abhinav feeling during the project call?
qa.a: Abhinav was starving and irritable, so everything felt annoying, and later felt sorry for being a jerk.

qa.q: What plan did Abhinav make?
qa.a: Eat before calls, say plainly when food has to come first, and apologise to Mitali.

qa.q: How might Mitali have felt when the idea was called dumb?
qa.a: Mitali probably felt hurt and embarrassed in front of the group.

grounding: A growing teenager gets sharp when meals are late and learns to say they need to eat before talking.

passage: By six in the evening, Mina and Abebe had been walking round Lisbon for seven hours with only coffee. When Mina suggested one more museum, Abebe snapped, 'Do you ever stop planning everything?' Mina went silent, cheeks hot. So that's what he really thinks of me, she thought. They walked to the tram stop without a word. Then Mina noticed Abebe's hands shaking slightly as he checked the map. 'When did you last eat?' she asked. 'Breakfast,' he admitted. They found a bakery and shared custard tarts and soup on a bench. Halfway through, Abebe said, 'I'm sorry. That was the hunger talking. Your plans made this trip.' They agreed to talk about the schedule tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Mina and Abebe share on the bench?
qa.a: Custard tarts and soup.

qa.q: What did Mina feel when Abebe snapped about planning?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, taking it personally as what he really thought of her.

qa.q: What helped them pause before the argument grew?
qa.a: Mina noticed the shaking hands and asked when he last ate; they ate first and left the schedule talk for tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Abebe see the moment after eating?
qa.a: He felt sorry, recognising that hunger had done the talking, and he valued Mina's plans after all.

grounding: A friend snapped at after a long day without food takes it personally until they eat first and revisit the issue later.
